name: T. E. Wood's survival-test cryptogram
ciphertext_source: Cipherbrain post 35 (Schmeh 2017, sources/schmeh/posts/35-thouless.txt), 'T. E. A Wood's cryptogram' section: 'In 1950 some T. E. Wood (born in 1887) from Bournemouth, UK, published the following cryptogram: FVAMI NTKFX XWATB OIZVV X'. Schmeh does not name the original publication venue (presumably a parapsychology journal following Thouless's 1948 example, since Wood is described as following Thouless's call for others to run the same experiment); this is inferred, not established, from context alone.
alphabet: Latin capitals A-Z, 21 letters, no spaces within groups (groups of 5 as printed, last group 1 letter)

constraints.method: same as Thouless's own cryptograms (Cipherbrain post 35, adjacent section): a keyed running-sum cipher. The key is a sequence of distinct words drawn from a book or published text (duplicates of earlier words in the sequence are dropped); each word's letters are summed A=1..Z=26 and reduced mod 26 to give one number per plaintext letter; that number is added (mod 26) to the plaintext letter to give the ciphertext letter.
constraints.wood_specific: Wood said his key text was 'a book, which is not written in English'; the plaintext is 'allegedly authored in several different languages' per Schmeh -- so neither the key language nor the plaintext language is English, unlike Thouless's own two cryptograms
constraints.precedent: Thouless's message A was solved within weeks of publication by conventional cryptanalysis (method not detailed in this post); Thouless's message C was solved in 1995 by Jim Gillogly via a dictionary attack that found the key text (Gillogly, 'Cryptograms from the Crypt', Cryptologia). Thouless's message B remains unsolved as of Schmeh's 2017 post. Wood's is a distinct, separately unsolved cryptogram by a different author using the same method, with an explicitly non-English key and plaintext.

cheap_tests_in_order: 1. Replicate Gillogly's successful method on Thouless message C (a dictionary attack over candidate key texts, computing the running-sum key and testing the resulting plaintext for a real word/phrase) against Wood's cryptogram, trying well-known non-English books first (major European-language Bibles, classic novels in French/German/Latin) as Wood's key text. At N=21 this is far too short for any statistical language judge to be informative on its own; treat a hit only as a candidate for manual inspection, never a score-based PASS. Cost $2, Sonnet.

2. Letter-frequency and index-of-coincidence profile of the 21 letters against English, French, German and Latin single-letter tables, more to rule out a same-language key+plaintext pairing than to identify one (21 letters is far below any reliable IC signal). Cost under $1.

3. Search whether T. E. Wood's original 1950 publication can be identified (parapsychology journal indexes, JSTOR/Google Books for 'Wood' + 'Thouless' + 1950), since knowing the venue narrows which non-English books a 1950 Bournemouth reader was likely to reach for. Cost $1-2 (print check).
matched_control: run 25 Sept 2026 (cheap_test_done.1): synthetic N=21 cryptogram, real English sentence + true running-sum key from de_novel_faust.txt at a random offset, searched over the same 0..20000-word range as the real attack; true offset ranked 1st of ~19,980 candidates in all 3 seeds (scores 19-20 of 21 vs runner-up 16-17)

1.method: specs/cheap-tests/te-wood-1950/gillogly_attack.py -- Gillogly-style dictionary attack: for each of 4 candidate key texts (French Bible, Latin Vulgate, French novel Les Miserables, German novel Faust -- fetched from archive.org, see README.md) and every start offset in the first 20,000 raw words, derive the N=21 running-sum key stream (first 21 distinct words from that offset, Thouless dedup rule), decrypt, score with tools/english_score.py EnglishModel.cover() (longest dictionary-word-segmentable stretch) against an English model and a model built from the key text's own language. Matched control: synthetic N=21 cryptogram from a real English sentence + the true key at a random offset in one key text (de_novel_faust.txt), same script, same 0..20000-word search range, 3 seeds.
1.control_verdict: true offset ranks 1st of ~19,980 candidates in all 3 seeds (scores 19-20/21 vs runner-up 16-17/21) -- method and scoring function demonstrably work.
1.target_verdict: best top-1 score per key text: fr_bible 12/21, la_vulgate 12/21, fr_novel 12/21, de_novel_faust 16/21 -- none reach the control's true-positive band (18-20/21), the best (16) sits below the control's own runner-up band, and no top-10 candidate in any of the 4 attack_*.txt files reads as a real sentence on inspection.
1.conclusion: no candidate found among these 4 key texts (first 20,000 words each): negative, not a lead worth manual inspection. A 5th candidate (1912 Luther Bible) 404'd on archive.org, not retried. Full method, limitations (word-count cap, untried key texts, single-language scoring blind to a 3rd language) and reproduce commands in specs/cheap-tests/te-wood-1950/README.md.
1.requests_per_host: archive.org: 17 (11 discovery -- 6 advancedsearch, 5 metadata; 6 download attempts, 1 of which 404'd), >=1.5s apart, one host only

value: low-medium: the method is fully understood and demonstrated to be solvable in two of the three known instances (Thouless A and C), but N=21 is extremely short and the key is explicitly non-English, so a corpus-based language check cannot gate a candidate here -- only a crib/dictionary-attack hit can
status_25_Sept_2026: open per Schmeh 2017; Thouless's own message B (a different, related cryptogram by the method's originator) is also still unsolved; Wood's death date unknown to Schmeh
schema_note: cheap_tests_in_order are proposals (rule 10: an approach is not a claim); a test actually run goes under cheap_test_done with its control. judge block omits 'language' deliberately: at N=21 with a non-English key and multi-lingual plaintext, tools/judge_plaintext.py's n-gram language check would be uninformative (the exact scenario the module's docstring calls a gate, not a proof) and could mislead; length is the only mechanical check that means anything here until a specific crib or key text is proposed (then add 'cribs' or 'cribs_at').
